Alan Bean (March 15, 1932 - May 26, 2018) was an American naval officer and aviator, aeronautical engineer, test pilot, NASA astronaut and painter.
United around 3150 BC by a ruler called Menes or Narmer, this Nile-valley civilization is considered one of the world's cradles of civilization — name it?
Ancient Egypt was a cradle of civilization concentrated along the lower reaches of the Nile River in the northeastern corner of Africa.

Asclepius (Ancient) is a hero and god of medicine in ancient Greek religion and mythology.
He was the principal organizer of the 1963 March on Washington and a leader for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights — which activist is it?
Bayard Rustin (March 17, 1912 - August 24, 1987) was an American political activist and prominent leader in social movements for civil rights, socialism, nonviolence, and gay rights.
This Turkish statesman and poet served as prime minister four separate times between 1974 and 2002, chairing first the Republican People's Party and later his own Democratic Left Party — who is he?
Bülent Ecevit (28 May 1925 - 5 November 2006) was a Turkish statesman, poet, writer, scholar, and journalist.

This Republican engineer, whose father once served as New Hampshire governor and White House chief of staff, was himself elected governor of that state four times, matching only one predecessor. Who is he?
Chris Sununu (s-; born November 5, 1974) is an American politician and engineer who served as the 82nd governor of New Hampshire from 2017 to 2025.

Henri de La Tour d'Auvergne, Viscount of Turenne
David Farragut (also spelled Glascoe; July 5, 1801 - August 14, 1870) was a flag officer of the United States Navy during the American Civil War.
This New Zealand mountaineer, alongside Tenzing Norgay, became the first climber confirmed to reach the summit of Mount Everest, on 29 May 1953 — who is he?
Edmund Hillary (20 July 1919 - 11 January 2008) was a New Zealand mountaineer, explorer, and philanthropist.

Robert Cecil, Viscount Cecil of Chelwood

Gallic Wars were waged between 58 and 50 BC by the Roman general Julius Caesar against the peoples of Gaul (present-day France, Belgium, and Switzerland).

This Russian mystic and faith healer gained enormous influence over the imperial family of Tsar Nicholas II in the final years of the empire. Born a Siberian peasant in 1869, he's best remembered for his mysterious sway over the fate of Russia itself — who is this controversial figure?
Grigori Rasputin was Russian mystic (1869–1916). Grigori Yefimovich Rasputin (21 January [O.S. 9 January] 1869 – 30 December [O.S. 17 December] 1916) was a Russian mystic and faith healer.
FDR's vice president from 1941 to 1945, this Iowa-born agriculture and commerce secretary later ran for the White House as the new Progressive Party's nominee in 1948 — who was he?
Henry A. Wallace (October 7, 1888 - November 18, 1965) was the 33rd vice president of the United States, serving from 1941 to 1945, under President Franklin D. Roosevelt.

A Scottish politician born to Pakistani immigrant parents became the youngest justice secretary in 2018, then health secretary, before leading his party and nation from March 2023 to May 2024. Who served as First Minister of Scotland?
Humza Yousaf (born 7 April 1985) is a Scottish politician who served as First Minister of Scotland and Leader of the Scottish National Party (SNP) from March 2023 to May 2024.
An anti-apartheid fighter who spent ten years on Robben Island, this man rose to lead the ANC and then served as South Africa's president from 2009 to 2018 — who is he?
Jacob Zuma (born 12 April 1942) is a South African politician who served as the president of South Africa from 2009 to 2018.

This West Virginia politician served as secretary of state, then governor, then US senator over a 24-year span, remaining a Democrat until switching to independent in 2024; he also co-founded a coal brokerage company. Who is he?
Joe Manchin (born August 24, 1947) is an American politician and businessman from West Virginia.
Succeeding Rowan Williams in 2013, this archbishop presided over the wedding of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle during a tenure that saw the church's first female bishop ordained — who is he?
Justin Welby (born 6 January 1956) is a retired Anglican bishop who served as the 105th archbishop of Canterbury in the Church of England from 2013 to 2025.
A former transplant surgeon nicknamed 'Ko P,' this Taiwanese politician served as mayor of Taipei before founding his own political party. Who is he?
Ko Wen-je (pinyin: K Wnzh; born 6 August 1959), also known by his nickname Ko P, is a Taiwanese politician, physician, and transplant surgeon who served as the 13th mayor of Taipei from 2014 to 2022.
Relieved from her post by the Secretary of Defense in 2025, this admiral had been the first woman to serve as chief of naval operations and the first woman on the Joint Chiefs of Staff — who is she?

Lisa Franchetti (fran-; born 25 April 1964) is a retired United States Navy admiral who served as the 33rd chief of naval operations from 2 November 2023 to 21 February 2025, after being relieved by Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth.
After representing Florida in the Senate for over a decade, this Republican politician became the nation's top diplomat and acting national security advisor in 2025 — who is he?
Marco Rubio (born May 28, 1971) is an American politician, attorney, and diplomat serving as the 72nd United States secretary of state since 2025.

Ruling the Franks from the mid-5th century until Pepin the Short's takeover in 751, this dynasty defeated the Visigoths in 507 and the Burgundians in 534 to build Western Europe's most powerful realm — which dynasty?
Merovingian dynasty was the ruling family of the Franks from around the middle of the 5th century until Pepin the Short in 751.

This Indian independence activist and politician served as prime minister from 1977 to 1979 leading the Janata Party government, after decades holding posts from Bombay's chief ministership to deputy prime minister — who is he?
Prince Albert Victor, Duke of Clarence and Avondale

Morarji Desai (29 February 1896 - 10 April 1995) was an Indian politician and independence activist who served as the prime minister of India between 1977 and 1979 leading the government formed by the Janata Party.

This Florentine diplomat served Florence's republic while the Medici were out of power, then wrote a slim political treatise — unpublished until five years after his death — that earned him the title 'father of modern political science.' Who was he?
Niccolò Machiavelli (3 May 1469 - 21 June 1527) was a Florentine diplomat, author, philosopher, and historian who lived during the Italian Renaissance.
Backed by the Byzantine emperor Zeno, this Germanic people's king invaded Italy and preserved Roman law and administration from his capital at Ravenna — who were they?
Ostrogoths were a Roman-era Germanic people who, in the 5th and 6th centuries, established one of the two major Gothic kingdoms within the Western Roman Empire.
This former Dutch MP, who focused on tax and pension policy, stepped away from politics in 2025 citing burnout after founding the New Social Contract party — who is he?
Alfred, Duke of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha

Pieter Omtzigt (born 8 January 1974) is a Dutch former politician who served as a member of the House of Representatives between 2003 and 2025 apart from a short interruption between June and October 2010.
Chair of the Senate Homeland Security Committee, this Kentucky Republican ran for his party's presidential nomination in 2016 — who is he?
Rand Paul (born January 7, 1963) is an American politician serving as the junior United States senator from Kentucky since 2011.

In 1941 this Deputy to the Führer made a bizarre solo flight to Scotland hoping to talk Britain out of the war — and ended up a prisoner, later dying by suicide at 93 while still serving a life sentence. Who was he?
Rudolf Hess (He in German; 26 April 1894 - 17 August 1987) was a German politician, convicted war criminal, and a leading member of the Nazi Party in Germany.
An Old Bolshevik and Politburo member who led the Communist Party in Leningrad, he was gunned down at his office in 1934 — an assassination Stalin used to launch the Great Purge. Who was he?
Sergei Kirov (born Kostrikov; 27 March 1886 - 1 December 1934) was a Russian and Soviet politician and Bolshevik revolutionary.
Founded by crusading knights along the Baltic during the 13th-century Northern Crusades, this theocratic realm at its peak stretched from Prussia to Estonia and included Gotland — what was it called?
State of the Teutonic Order was a theocratic state located along the southeastern shore of the Baltic Sea in northern Europe.

This ancient Indo-European-speaking people inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe, in territory spanning modern Bulgaria, Romania, and northern Greece, as well as parts of northwestern Anatolia — who were they?
Thracians were an Indo-European-speaking people who inhabited large parts of Southeast Europe in ancient history. The Thracian culture emerged during the early Bronze Age, which began about 3500 BC.
This Argentine lawyer and conservative politician has served as her country's vice president since 2023, having founded a legal-studies center focused on terrorism victims. Who is she?
Victoria Villarruel (born 13 April 1975) is an Argentine politician, lawyer, writer, and activist who has served as the 38th vice president of Argentina since 2023.

Co-founder of the Center for Constitutional Rights and defender of the Chicago Seven, this attorney was dubbed by The New York Times 'the country's most controversial and, perhaps, its best-known lawyer.' Who?
William Kunstler (July 7, 1919 - September 4, 1995) was an American attorney and civil rights activist, known for defending the Chicago Seven.
Centered on the Avesta and the teachings of an ancient Iranian prophet, this faith — among the world's oldest organized religions — reveres a supreme deity named Ahura Mazda — name the religion?
Zoroastrianism is an Iranian religion centred on the Avesta and the teachings of Zarathushtra Spitama, who is more commonly referred to by the Greek translation, Zoroaster (Ancient).
Traditionally chanted by a muezzin from a mosque's minaret before each of the five daily prayers, what is this Islamic call known as?
Adhan: Islamic call to prayer. The five prayer times are known in Arabic as fajr (فجر), dhuhr (ظهر), asr (عصر), maghrib (مغرب), and isha (عشاء).
A criminal-law professor who earned his law degree at 24, this Peronist served as Argentina's longest-tenured Cabinet Chief before becoming the country's president from 2019 to 2023 — who is he?

Alberto Fernández: President of Argentina from 2019 to 2023. Born in Buenos Aires, Fernández attended the University of Buenos Aires, where he earned his law degree at age 24, and later became a professor of criminal law.
In 2024, this Manhattan district attorney became the first person to secure a criminal conviction of a former U.S. president — who is he?
Alvin Bragg: American lawyer and politician (born 1973)

Anne Boleyn: Queen of England from 1533 to 1536.

Assassination of Uthman: 656 murder of the third Rashidun caliph in Medina.

Battle of Alesia: Part of the Gallic Wars.

Bhumibol Adulyadej: King of Thailand from 1946 to 2016.

Bülent Ecevit: Prime Minister of Turkey (1974; 1977; 1978–79; 1999–2002)

Cevdet Yılmaz: Vice President of Turkey since 2023. Cevdet Yılmaz (born 1 April 1967) is a Turkish politician who has been the 2nd and current vice president of Turkey since 2023.
This South Korean general seized power after the 1979 assassination of the country's previous dictator, then declared martial law and became the nation's fifth president — who is he?
Chun Doo-hwan: Leader of South Korea from 1979 to 1988.

Crown of Castile: Former country in the Iberian Peninsula from 1230 to 1715.

Demeter: Greek goddess of the harvest, grains, and agriculture.

First Liberian Civil War: 1989–1997 war in West Africa.

Frigg: Germanic goddess. The names ultimately stem from the Proto-Germanic theonym *Frijjō.

Germanwings Flight 9525: 2015 deliberate aircraft crash in France.
A former dentist and health minister who became Turkmenistan's second president in 2006, he later struck a power-sharing deal handing the presidency to his son Serdar — who is he?
Gurbanguly Berdimuhamedow: President of Turkmenistan from 2007 to 2022.
Reigning from 786 to 809 as the fifth Abbasid caliph, this ruler founded Baghdad's House of Wisdom and ushered in what's considered the start of the Islamic Golden Age — who was he?

Hezbollah: Islamist movement and militant group based in Lebanon.
Inheriting a vast British property estate from his father in 2016, this aristocrat ranked 14th on the 2025 Sunday Times Rich List with a fortune nearing £9.9 billion — who is he?
Hugh Grosvenor, 7th Duke of Westminster: British aristocrat (born 1991)

Iran–Iraq War: 1980–1988 armed conflict in West Asia.
Guided by 24 tirthankaras who conquered the cycle of rebirth, this Indian religion built its entire ethical code on strict nonviolence to all living things — which faith?
Jainism: Indian religion. The community supported networks of temples, libraries, and charitable institutions.
Expelled from the Labour Party in 2024 after standing as an independent, which British politician had earlier led that party and the Opposition from 2015 to 2020?
After an unsuccessful mission to Georgia and a life-changing 1738 conversion experience, this English cleric founded the revival movement that became known as Methodism — who was he?
Roman emperor from 527 to 565, his dream of restoring the empire saw his general Belisarius reclaim North Africa, Italy and Rome from the Ostrogoths — who was he?
Justinian I: Roman emperor from 527 to 565. The praetorian prefect Liberius reclaimed the south of the Iberian Peninsula, establishing the province of Spania.

This semi-nomadic Turkic people built a major trading empire from the 6th century CE, dominating the Volga-Don steppes, Crimea, and the Caucasus for roughly three centuries as a crossroads on the Silk Road?
Khazars: Historical semi-nomadic Turkic ethnic group.
The son of a former Greek prime minister himself, who has led Greece's centre-right governing party since 2016 and served as PM since 2019?
Kyriakos Mitsotakis: Prime Minister of Greece (2019–2023; since 2023). Mitsotakis has been president of the New Democracy party since 2016.
Raised by Zhou Enlai after his revolutionary father was executed, this politician served as China's premier from 1987 to 1998 — who is it?
Li Peng: Premier of China from 1987 to 1998. For much of the 1990s Li was ranked second in the Chinese Communist Party (CCP) hierarchy behind then CCP General Secretary Jiang Zemin.
This American activist began on the far left, swung to the far right in the 1970s, ran for president again and again, and founded a movement often likened to a cult — who is he?

Mansur Yavaş: Turkish politician and mayor of Ankara.

This retired U.S. Army lieutenant general served just 22 days as national security advisor before resigning over reports he misled officials about talks with Russia's ambassador — who is he?
Michael Flynn: U.S. Army general and former U.S. National Security Advisor (born 1958)

N. Chandrababu Naidu: 13th Chief Minister of Andhra Pradesh (born 1950)
The first Indian American to serve in a presidential cabinet, this politician was South Carolina's governor and then the UN ambassador under Donald Trump. Who is she?
Nikki Haley: American politician and diplomat (born 1972)
A brigadier general who seized power in a 1989 coup and ruled Sudan under various titles until a 2019 coup toppled him, after which he was jailed and convicted of corruption — who is he?
Omar al-Bashir: President of Sudan from 1989 to 2019.

Paul Keating: Prime Minister of Australia from 1991 to 1996.
India's longest-serving Minister of Commerce and Industry, this politician also won the 2018 Carnot Prize for his work in energy policy — who is he?

Taken as a Mughal hostage at age nine to enforce his father's treaty, this man later ruled from 1681 to 1689 as the second king of a major Indian empire — who is he?

Selim II: Sultan of the Ottoman Empire from 1566 to 1574.
Eldest daughter of King Amalric, this 12th-century ruler stood by her unpopular husband Guy of Lusignan even as her leprosy-stricken brother struggled to secure her succession — who is she?
Sibylla, Queen of Jerusalem: Crusader ruler from 1186 to 1190.

On 26 September 1983, this Soviet duty officer judged his early-warning system's report of incoming U.S. missiles to be a false alarm — disobeying protocol and likely averting nuclear war. Who was he?
Stanislav Petrov: Soviet Air Defence Forces officer (1939–2017)

Taishō era: Period of Japanese history from 1912 to 1926.
Serving as Lord Chancellor before becoming Archbishop of Canterbury, this cleric clashed with King Henry II and was murdered by the king's men in 1170 — who was he?
Thomas Becket: Archbishop of Canterbury from 1162 to 1170.

Despite a huge edge in tanks and aircraft, the Soviet Union took heavy losses and was expelled from the League of Nations after its November 1939 invasion of Finland — what was this three-and-a-half-month conflict called?
Winter War: 1939–1940 war between the Soviet Union and Finland.
A career Army general who became a national hero in the Mexican-American War, this 12th U.S. president died of a stomach illness just 16 months into office — who is he?
Zachary Taylor: President of the United States from 1849 to 1850.

Carl Wilhelm Scheele is a chemist. Carl Wilhelm Scheele (German: [ˈʃeːlə], Swedish: [ˈɧêːlɛ]; 9 December 1742 – 21 May 1786) was a German-Swedish pharmaceutical chemist.
What is the atomic number of Oganesson?
Oganesson is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Og and atomic number 118.
In what year was Pythagoras born?
Pythagoras: Pythagoras of Samos (Ancient Greek: Πυθαγόρας; c. 570 – c. 495 BC) was an ancient Ionian Greek philosopher, polymath, and the eponymous founder of Pythagoreanism.
In what year did Srinivasa Ramanujan die?
Srinivasa Ramanujan Iyengar (22 December 1887 – 26 April 1920) was an Indian mathematician who worked during the early 20th century.
In what year was Silicon discovered?
Silicon (SILL-ih-kən) is a chemical element; it has symbol Si and atomic number 14.
Which company manufactures Antonov An-124 Ruslan?
Antonov An-124 Ruslan: Aviastar-SP. The An-124 remains the largest military transport aircraft in service.
In which country is Dassault Rafale based?
Dassault Rafale: France. Dassault built a technology demonstrator that first flew in July 1986 as part of an eight-year flight-test programme, paving the way for approval of the project.
Who is credited with discovering Horologium?

Horologium (constellation): Nicolas Louis de Lacaille. It was first described by the French astronomer Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille in 1756 and visualized by him as a clock with a pendulum and a second hand.
Who is credited with discovering Hubble's law?
Hubble's law: Georges Lemaître. The Friedmann equations showed the universe might be expanding, and presented the expansion speed if that were the case.
Who is credited with discovering Eris?
Eris (dwarf planet): Michael E. Brown. Eris (minor-planet number 136199) is the most massive and second-largest known dwarf planet in the Solar System.
Hiding in coffee, fresh bread, and ripe fruit, this aldehyde is also what your liver makes when breaking down alcohol — and a prime culprit behind the morning-after hangover. What is it?
Acetaldehyde (IUPAC systematic name ethanal) is an organic chemical compound with the formula CH3CH=O.
This genus of more than 650 flowering succulent species includes a 'true' member cultivated worldwide as the standard source for a soothing pharmaceutical gel — what's the genus?
Aloe (also written Alo) is a genus containing over 650 species of flowering succulent plants.
Whether contracted through the skin, the lungs, or the gut, this Bacillus-driven infection can take up to two months to show symptoms — what is it?
Anthrax is an infection caused by the bacterium Bacillus anthracis or Bacillus cereus biovar anthracis.
This common vision condition occurs when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped rather than spherical, causing blurred vision at any distance. What is it?
Astigmatism is a type of refractive error due to rotational asymmetry in the eye's refractive power.
This steel-gray, lightweight metal with atomic number 4 is found in gemstones like aquamarine and emerald, but within the cores of stars it gets destroyed as fast as it forms — what element is it?
Beryllium is a chemical element; it has symbol Be and atomic number 4.
First described in 1903 from fossils found in Colorado, this sauropod dinosaur's Greek name means arm lizard, a reference to its proportionately long front limbs — what genus is it?
Brachiosaurus is a genus of sauropod dinosaur that lived in North America during the Late Jurassic, about 155.6 to 145.5 million years ago.
This group of diseases involves uncontrolled cell growth, includes over 100 types, and is responsible for about 33% of deaths when linked to tobacco and alcohol. What disease are we discussing?
Cancer is a group of diseases involving uncontrolled cell growth typically resulting in tumors with the potential to invade or spread to other parts of the body.
Also known by the taxonomic synonym Epilobium, this hardy perennial in the willowherb family is native throughout the temperate north — which plant?
Chamaenerion angustifolium is a perennial herbaceous flowering plant in the willowherb family, Onagraceae.
This neurological disorder strikes one side of the head around the eye and temple, often at the very same hour each day for an 8-to-10-week stretch before vanishing for months — what condition is it?
Cluster headache is a neurological disorder characterized by episodes of severe headaches on one side of the head, typically around the eye and temple, lasting between 15 minutes to three hours.
Native to Europe and Western Asia, this birch-family shrub produces the round nuts sold commercially as hazelnuts — which species?
Corylus avellana is a species of flowering plant in the birch family Betulaceae.

This common cough suppressant found in cold medicine was combined with bupropion in 2022 to create a fast-acting antidepressant, despite belonging to the same chemical class as morphine — what drug is it?
Dextromethorphan is a cough suppressant used in many cough and cold medicines.
Named from Greek roots meaning 'to repeat' and 'speech,' this automatic repetition of another person's vocalizations is closely related to echopraxia, the repeating of movements. What is it called?
Echolalia is the repetition of vocalizations made by another person; when repeated by the same person, it is called palilalia.
This American physicist won a Nobel Prize for inventing a particle accelerator and later worked on uranium-isotope separation for the Manhattan Project. Who is he?
Ernest Lawrence (August 8, 1901 - August 27, 1958) was an American physicist who received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1939 for his invention of the cyclotron.
This body part is a prominent, usually flexible digit found on the forelimbs of most four-limbed vertebrates — on the hind limbs, the equivalent shorter digits are instead called toes. What is it?
Finger is a prominent digit on the forelimbs of most tetrapod vertebrate animals, especially those with prehensile extremities (i.e.
First studied scientifically by an Augustinian friar experimenting with pea plants in 19th-century Brno, this branch of biology examines heredity and trait inheritance — which field?
Genetics is the study of genes, genetic variation, and heredity in organisms.
In this rapid-onset condition the immune system attacks the peripheral nerves, so weakness creeps up from the feet and hands — and about 15% of patients need a ventilator. What is it?
Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS) is a rapid-onset muscle weakness caused by the immune system damaging the peripheral nervous system.

The reciprocal cross to the more common mule, this equine hybrid is the offspring of a male horse and a female donkey, differing from its counterpart in both physiology and temperament — what is it called?
Hinny is a domestic equine hybrid, the offspring of a male horse (a stallion) and a female donkey (a jenny).

This phenomenon describes how a system's state depends on its history, as when a magnet holds different moments depending on past field changes — it underlies memory in a hard disk drive. What is it called?
Hysteresis is the dependence of the state of a system on its history. Hysteresis can be found in physics, chemistry, engineering, biology, and economics.

This American physicist worked on the Manhattan Project, then in 1949 proposed that — contrary to belief — not all atomic nuclei are spherical, an idea Aage Bohr later helped confirm. Who won a share of the 1975 Nobel for it?
James Rainwater (December 9, 1917 - May 31, 1986) was an American physicist who shared the Nobel Prize in Physics in 1975 for his part in determining the asymmetrical shapes of certain atomic nuclei.
Linked to a herpesvirus and immune suppression, this cancer causing purple skin lesions was already being described by Hippocrates in the 300s BC — which condition?
Kaposi's sarcoma (KS) is a type of cancer that can form masses on the skin, in lymph nodes, in the mouth, or in other organs.
Representing the Nemean Lion slain by Heracles as one of his twelve labors, this zodiac constellation sits between Cancer and Virgo — which constellation?
Leo (constellation) is one of the constellations of the zodiac, between Cancer, the Crab, to the west and Virgo, the Maiden, to the east.
Credited as the 'Father of Cinematography' for filming Roundhay Garden Scene in Leeds in 1888, this French inventor mysteriously vanished in 1890 before cinema took off — who was he?

Louis Le Prince (28 August 1841 - disappeared 16 September 1890; declared dead 16 September 1897) was a French artist and the inventor of an early motion-picture camera, and director of Roundhay Garden Scene.
This Italian economist served as prime minister from 2021 to 2022 after previously heading the European Central Bank for eight years and the Bank of Italy before that — who is he?

Mario Draghi (born 3 September 1947) is an Italian politician, economist, academic, banker, statesman, and civil servant, who served as the prime minister of Italy from 13 February 2021 to 22 October 2022.
This medical condition is diagnosed when the erect length of the affected organ measures at least two and a half standard deviations below the average size for age — what condition is it?
Micropenis is an unusually small penis.
With shells that are elongated and wedge-shaped rather than round, these bivalves attach themselves to shorelines using threads nicknamed a "beard" — what are they?
Mussel is the common name used for members of several families of bivalve molluscs, from saltwater and freshwater habitats.
Catalyzed in nature by iron-bearing nitrogenase enzymes and famously partnered with legumes, this process turns molecular N2 into ammonia — what's it called?
Nitrogen fixation is a chemical process by which molecular dinitrogen (N2) is converted into ammonia (NH3).
All 14 species of this slim-bodied, dense-furred mammal are semiaquatic, and they're famous for playful antics like sliding into the water and juggling stones — what is it?
Otter are carnivorous mammals in the subfamily Lutrinae.
It comes in a G version for the needle and a V version for the mouth, and it owes its name to the very mould it's coaxed from — which medication?
Penicillin (PCN or PEN) are a group of beta-lactam antibiotics originally obtained from Penicillium moulds, principally P. chrysogenum.
This scientific term for a group of fin-footed, mostly marine mammals includes walruses, sea lions, fur seals, and true earless seals — 34 living species in all. What is the term?
Pinniped are a widely distributed and diverse clade of carnivorous, fin-footed, semiaquatic, mostly marine mammals.
Bloating, mood swings, breast tenderness and irritability that flare in the week or two before menstruation and fade once bleeding begins — what disruptive condition is this?
Premenstrual syndrome (PMS) is a disruptive set of emotional and physical symptoms that regularly occur in the one to two weeks before the start of each menstrual period.

Named for the ragged appearance of its leaves, this genus of flowering plants native mainly to North America has become an invasive nuisance in parts of Europe due to climate change — what plant is it?
Ragweed are flowering plants in the genus Ambrosia in the aster family, Asteraceae.

This long-term skin condition causes facial redness, pimples, and swelling, and can lead to a severely enlarged, reddened nose in extreme cases — its exact cause remains unknown — name this condition?
Rosacea is a long-term skin condition that typically affects the face.
About 950 species of these spiny, globe-shaped marine animals crawl the seabed on tube feet, found from tide pools down to 5,000 metres deep. What are they?
Sea urchin are the class Echinoidea within the echinoderms.
Pythons and boas of this limbless reptile group still carry a tiny pelvic girdle and vestigial leg-stubs near the cloaca, hinting at long-lost legs. What animal is this?
Snake are elongated legless reptiles of the suborder Serpentes.
A small Eurasian mustelid that turns brilliant white in winter, this animal's coat — known as ermine — once draped Catholic monarchs and the Infant Jesus of Prague — what is it?
Stoat (Mustela erminea), also known as the Eurasian ermine or ermine, is a species of mustelid native to Eurasia and the northern regions of North America.
Named for a U.S. state where its discovery research was based, this synthetic element (symbol Ts) holds the second-highest atomic number of all and was the most recently discovered — what is it?
Tennessine is a synthetic element; it has symbol Ts and atomic number 117.

This parasite can infect nearly any warm-blooded animal, but can only sexually reproduce inside cats, and is famous for altering infected rodents' behavior to make them less afraid of feline predators — what parasite is it?
Toxoplasma gondii is a species of parasitic alveolate that causes toxoplasmosis.
Just 25 light-years away, this is the brightest star in the constellation Lyra and the fifth-brightest star in the entire night sky — what is it?
Vega is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Lyra. It has the Bayer designation α Lyrae, which is Latinised to Alpha Lyrae and abbreviated Alpha Lyr or α Lyr.
Chairman of the Polish People's Party since 2015 and a former Minister of Labour and Social Affairs, this physician-turned-politician ran for the Polish presidency in 2020 — who is he?
Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz (born 10 August 1981) is a Polish physician and politician, who has served as the Deputy Prime Minister of Poland, and Minister of National Defence since 2023.
Unearthed in Montana by Jack Horner's team in 1987, this 20-foot horned dinosaur sported a bony neck-frill and lived roughly 75 million years ago — which species?
Achelousaurus: Genus of ceratopsid dinosaur from North America.
Often called the father of theoretical computer science, this Englishman gave us a famous 'machine' that formalized the very idea of computation — who was he?
Nicknamed 'whip-spiders' or 'tailless whip-scorpions,' these arachnids have no silk, no venom, and a name meaning 'blunt tail' — they grab with their pedipalps instead of biting — what order is this?
Amblypygi: Order of arachnids. The name "amblypygid" means "blunt tail", a reference to a lack of the flagellum that is otherwise seen in whip-scorpions.
Brought to Asia by Spanish traders aboard the Manila galleons, this tropical American tree produces a knobby, sweet fruit known as sugar apple or custard apple — what is this plant?
Annona squamosa: Species of tree. Annona squamosa is a small, well-branched tree or shrub from the family Annonaceae that bears edible fruits called sugar apples or sweetsops or custard apples.
Its guanidino group serves as the biological precursor for nitric oxide production, and this amino acid earned the one-letter code 'R' purely for phonetic reasons — what is it?
Arginine: Amino acid. Arginine is the amino acid with the formula (H2N)(HN)CN(H)(CH2)3CH(NH2)CO2H.
From the Greek for "self-devouring," this lysosome-driven process lets a cell tidily break down and recycle its own worn-out parts — what is it?
Autophagy: Process of cells digesting parts of themselves.
Sometimes called the common, lawn, or English variety, this European plant is considered the archetypal member of the daisy family — what's its scientific name?

Bellis perennis: Species of plant in the daisy family. Bellis perennis ( BEL-iss pə-REN-iss), the daisy, is a European species of the family Asteraceae, often considered the archetypal species of the name daisy.
This small, fluid-filled pocket that forms in the skin's upper layers — usually from friction, burns, or infection — gets the name 'bleb' when it's especially tiny. What is it?
Blister: Small pocket of fluid within the upper layers of the skin. The word "blister" entered English in the 14th century.

Originating from feral Eastern Mediterranean populations, this single wild plant species has been cultivated into an astonishing range of vegetables including broccoli, cauliflower, kale, and Brussels sprouts. What is it?
Brassica oleracea: Species of plant. Brassica oleracea, also known as wild cabbage in its uncultivated form, is a plant of the family Brassicaceae.
The world's most widely consumed psychoactive substance works by mimicking adenosine's shape and blocking its receptors, keeping you awake — what is this stimulant?

This German-Swedish pharmacist had a knack for discovery — molybdenum, tungsten, barium, chlorine, and arguably oxygen all trace to his bench — but the same hands-on chemistry may have killed him via mercury poisoning. Which unlucky genius is it?
Carl Wilhelm Scheele: Swedish German chemist who discovered oxygen (1742–1786)
Descended from land mammals but now fully aquatic, this group swims via up-and-down tail strokes and includes toothed members capable of echolocation — what group includes whales and dolphins?
Known for an exceptionally loud song produced by rapid buckling of drum-like tymbals, some periodical members of this insect superfamily emerge en masse only every 13 or 17 years — which insect?
Cicada: Superfamily of insects. The cicadas are a superfamily, the Cicadoidea, of insects in the order Hemiptera (true bugs).
This umbrella term covers mental processes like perception, attention, memory, and reasoning that let us acquire and apply knowledge — what is it called?
Cognition: Mental process dealing with knowledge.
This mostly inactive steroid hormone is created when an enzyme shields organs like the kidneys by converting active cortisol into its inactive form — what is it?
Cortisone: Corticosteroid precursor and metabolite of cortisol.
Started in 1955 by an army colonel and a cynologist as an experiment, this hybrid dog breed became officially recognized as a national breed in 1982 — which one?
Czechoslovakian Wolfdog: Czech and Slovak breed of dog.
Defined as having at least three loose or watery bowel movements in a single day, this condition is most often caused by an intestinal infection from contaminated food or water — what is it?

Diarrhea: Loose or liquid bowel movements. Diarrhea (American English), also spelled diarrhoea (British English), is the condition of having at least three loose, liquid, or watery bowel movements in a day.
Smaller and shorter-necked than their swan and goose cousins in the family Anatidae, these aquatic birds are often confused with grebes, loons, and coots — what are they?
Duck: Common name for many species of bird.
The first woman admitted to MIT, this environmental chemist was the first to apply chemistry to nutrition and founded the home economics movement — who was she?
Ellen Swallow Richards: American engineer and chemist (1843–1911)
The major female sex hormone, this estrogen drives the development of secondary sexual characteristics and helps maintain reproductive tissues from puberty through pregnancy — what is it?
Known for its smooth silvery-grey bark and toxin-laced but edible nuts, this deciduous tree native to Europe includes the striking copper-leaved cultivar among its ornamentals — which species?
Fagus sylvatica: Species of deciduous tree. It is native to much of Europe, growing in humid climates.
Lacking a body cavity and equipped with just one opening for both eating and excreting, these simple unsegmented invertebrates are named for their shape — what are they?
Found in the rainforests and savannas of sub-Saharan Africa, this snake has the longest fangs of any venomous species — up to two inches — and the highest venom yield of any snake — which snake?
Gaboon viper: Species of snake. It is the largest member of the genus Bitis.
The only venomous lizard native to the United States, this sluggish reptile from the Southwest rarely poses a real threat despite its fearsome reputation — what is it?
Gila monster: Largest species of lizard in the United States.

Native from Mexico down to southern Brazil, this large arboreal lizard can grow past six feet long, is a popular but demanding pet, and has become invasive in many warm regions worldwide — which species?
Green iguana: Species of reptile. Usually, this animal is simply called the iguana.

Named after a bird of prey, this British-developed attack aircraft was the only truly successful vertical-takeoff design of its era, able to fly from car parks and forest clearings instead of vulnerable airbases — which aircraft?
Harrier jump jet: Multirole combat aircraft family by Hawker Siddeley, later British Aerospace.
Hardy enough to survive winters as cold as -43°C, this shrub genus's aggressive roots fight soil erosion, and its berries and leaves are turned into food and skincare products — which genus?
Hippophae: Genus of flowering plants including sea buckthorn.
This huge insect order includes sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants, and its females often carry an egg-laying tube that doubles as a stinger — what order is it?
Hymenoptera: Order of insects. Over 150,000 living species of Hymenoptera have been described, in addition to over 2,000 extinct ones.
An application of computer science, this field covers not just computers and networks but also distribution technologies like television and telephones — what is it?
Information technology: Computer-based technologies. Whisler commented that "the new technology does not yet have a single established name.
Sometimes called the founder of pneumatic chemistry, this 17th-century Brussels physician coined the word 'gas' and ran a famous five-year willow-tree experiment. Who was he?
Jan Baptist van Helmont: Chemist and physician (1580–1644)
Equal to the work done when a one-newton force moves an object one metre, this SI unit of energy is named for a 19th-century English physicist — which unit?
Joule: SI unit of energy. The joule ( JOOL, or JOWL; symbol: J) is the unit of energy in the International System of Units (SI).
This colorless noble gas defined the length of the metre from 1960 to 1983, based on the wavelength of one of its spectral lines — which element?
Krypton: Chemical element with atomic number 36 (Kr)

Originally cultivated by the ancient Egyptians and now grown worldwide with China producing over half the crop, this leafy Asteraceae vegetable also has a stem-focused variety called celtuce — name the vegetable?
Lettuce: Species of annual plant of the daisy family, most often grown as a leaf vegetable.
Also called dragon's eye, this tropical fruit tree from the soapberry family produces fruit similar to lychee but with a milder aroma, and is native to Southeast Asia and southern China — what is it?
Longan: Species of tropical fruit-bearing tree.
Transmitted through the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes and caused by single-celled Plasmodium parasites, which disease's symptoms typically begin 10 to 15 days after infection?

Selected in 1969 as a dedicated air-superiority fighter and first flown in 1972, this twin-engine American jet boasts a staggering combat record of 106 victories and zero losses — which aircraft is it?
McDonnell Douglas F-15 Eagle: Multirole and air superiority fighter family.
Sold as Flagyl, this antibiotic and antiprotozoal fights everything from giardiasis to trichomoniasis — but it's notorious for leaving a metallic taste in your mouth — what is it?
Metronidazole: Antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication. Metronidazole, sold under the brand name Flagyl and Metrogyl among others, is an antibiotic and antiprotozoal medication.
Nicknamed 'water warts,' this viral skin infection causes small pink bumps with a telltale dimple in the center and usually clears up on its own within a year — what is it?

Molluscum contagiosum: Viral infection of the skin. Molluscum contagiosum (MC), sometimes called water warts, is a viral infection of the skin that results in small raised pink lesions with a dimple in the center.
In this group of bone-marrow cancers, blood cells fail to mature into healthy ones, and some cases progress into acute myeloid leukemia — what is it called?
Myelodysplastic syndrome: Diverse collection of blood-related cancers.
Unlike its niacin cousin, this form of vitamin B3 treats pellagra without causing skin flushing, and as a cream is used to fade acne scars and reduce hyperpigmentation — what is it?

Symbolized by the Greek letter omega, this SI unit of electrical resistance was named after a 19th-century German physicist and, since 2019, is defined as an exact value based on fundamental constants — what unit is it?
Ohm: SI derived unit of electrical resistance. The ohm (symbol: Ω, the uppercase Greek letter omega) is the unit of electrical resistance in the International System of Units (SI).
Sold in extended-release form under the brand name OxyContin, this highly addictive semi-synthetic opioid treats moderate to severe pain and brings relief within about fifteen minutes. What is it?
Oxycodone: Opioid medication. It is usually taken orally, and is available in immediate-release and controlled-release formulations.
Prized wood from this fruit tree's genus, Pyrus, is a favorite material for making high-quality woodwind instruments, and China grows about three-quarters of the world's crop — which fruit?
Pear: Edible fruits from the genus Pyrus.

First described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, this family of over 2,000 araneomorph spiders includes the "cellar spider" and "vibrating spider" — and shares a famous leggy nickname with harvestmen and crane flies. What family is it?
Pholcidae: Family of spiders. The family, first described by Carl Ludwig Koch in 1850, is divided into 94 genera.
Sometimes called a 'collapsed lung,' this condition involves air trapped in the space between the lung and chest wall, causing sudden sharp one-sided chest pain — what is it?
Pneumothorax: Abnormal collection of air in the pleural space.
This beta blocker treats high blood pressure and performance anxiety alike, and can even shrink capillary hemangiomas in infants — what drug?
Propranolol: Beta blocker drug. It can be taken orally, rectally, or by intravenous injection.
First identified in the 1950s as a radio source, this extremely luminous galactic nucleus can outshine an entire galaxy like the Milky Way thousands of times over — what is it?
Quasar: Active galactic nucleus (AGN) containing a supermassive black hole.
Often compared to the film in a camera, this innermost, light-sensitive layer of the eye sends signals along the optic nerve to the visual cortex — what is it?
Retina: Part of the eye. The retina (from Latin rete 'net'; pl. retinae or retinas) is the innermost, light-sensitive layer of tissue of the eye.
Once used by German butchers to herd cattle and pull meat carts to market, this mastiff-type breed now works as a search-and-rescue and police dog — which breed?
Rottweiler: Large German dog breed. The Rottweiler (UK also, German: [ˈʁɔtvaɪ̯lɐ]) is a breed of domestic mastiff type dog, regarded as medium-to-large or large.
Named after the Latin word for a small shovel, this flat triangular bone connects the upper arm bone to the collarbone and forms the back of the shoulder girdle — what is it?
Scapula: Bone that connects the humerus and clavicle.

Though crustaceans within this food category are more closely related to insects and spiders than to true fish, what group — including molluscs, crustaceans, and echinoderms — ranks among the most common food allergens?
Shellfish: Culinary and fisheries term for exoskeleton-bearing aquatic invertebrates.
Once called 'hyposulphite of soda,' this reducing agent treats cyanide poisoning and served as photography's key fixer in the 19th century — what compound?
Sodium thiosulfate: Chemical compound. Sodium thiosulfate (sodium thiosulphate) is an inorganic compound with the formula Na2S2O3·xH2O.
This English clergyman was the first person ever to measure blood pressure, and on the side he invented a ventilator and even wrote a tract against drinking — who was he?
Stephen Hales: English clergyman and scientist (1677–1761)
Derived from a Greek word meaning 'concurrence,' this medical term describes a set of signs and symptoms that tend to occur together — what is it called?
Syndrome: Association of several clinically recognizable features.
Also called oxolane, this colorless, water-miscible cyclic ether is a versatile solvent and polymer precursor — and an isomer of butanone. Abbreviated with three letters, what is it?
Discovered in Cornwall in 1791 and named after the Titans of Greek myth, this corrosion-resistant transition metal shrugs off seawater, aqua regia, and chlorine alike — what is it?
Titanium: Chemical element with atomic number 22 (Ti)

These simple-looking marine invertebrates surprise biologists: their tadpole-like larvae sport a notochord and dorsal nerve cord, making them startlingly close kin to vertebrates. What are these chordates?
Tunicate: Marine animals, subphylum of chordates.
Described from Mongolian fossils in 1924 and smaller than relatives like Deinonychus, which feathered, sickle-clawed dinosaur genus roamed Late Cretaceous Asia?
Velociraptor: Genus of Late Cretaceous dinosaur. The type species is V. mongoliensis, named and described in 1924.
First cultivated in the Fertile Crescent around 9600 BC, this cereal grass is grown on more land worldwide than any other food crop — which grain?
Wheat: Genus of grass cultivated for grain. Wheat is a group of wild and domesticated grasses of the genus Triticum.

Distinguished by a fatty hump on its shoulders and a large dewlap, this heat-tolerant type of domestic cattle originated in South Asia and holds religious significance in parts of the world — what is it?
Zebu: South Asian domestic cattle. The zebu (Bos indicus), also known as indicine cattle and humped cattle, is a species or subspecies of domestic cattle originating in South Asia.
The symbol for dubnium is Db. Dubnium is a synthetic chemical element; it has symbol Db and atomic number 105.
The symbol for barium is Ba. Barium is a chemical element; it has symbol Ba and atomic number 56.

Halle Berry: Halle Maria Berry ( HAL-ee; born Maria Halle Berry; August 14, 1966) is an American actress.
In what year was Liza Minnelli born?
Liza Minnelli: Liza May Minnelli ( LY-zə; born March 12, 1946) is an American actress, singer, and dancer.

Robert Duvall: Duvall won the Academy Award for Best Actor for his performance as an alcoholic former country music star in Tender Mercies (1983).
In what year was Rob Schneider born?
Rob Schneider: Robert Michael Schneider ( SHNY-dər; born October 31, 1963) is an American actor and comedian.

Jenna Ortega: Jenna Marie Ortega (born September 27, 2002) is an American actress.

Anne Heche: Heche's profile rose in 1997 with appearances in Donnie Brasco, Volcano, I Know What You Did Last Summer, and Wag the Dog.

Nick Cannon: Nicholas Scott Cannon (born October 8, 1980) is an American comedian, actor, and rapper.
